# Identifying and Removing Reverse Thread Drain Plugs

If you are staring at a concave or reverse-threaded oil drain plug, your first instinct might be to panic or assume you have the wrong tool. The geometry is deceptive: from the top down, it looks like a standard hex head bolt. You apply torque in the clockwise direction, and intuitively, that should tighten anything. However, this specific design feature, often found on older Subarus and certain European vehicles, uses a reverse thread to prevent accidental loosening during high-heat cycles or if the vehicle is jolted while parked.

The technical challenge here isn't mechanical failure; it's a mismatch between standard torque direction and the actual bolt rotation required for removal. The solution requires identifying the specific plug type before applying force. These plugs are frequently referred to as "reverse thread" or "anti-loosening" plugs. When searching for replacement gaskets or new bolts, you must explicitly specify that the plug has a reverse thread. Searching generic terms like "Subaru oil drain plug" without this qualifier often leads to purchasing parts with standard threads, which will either not install correctly or strip immediately upon tightening.

To remove the existing plug safely, you need a specialized socket. A standard 12-point socket can work if it has a magnetic base and a deep enough reach, but the most reliable method involves a specific "reverse thread" adapter or a socket with an internal spring mechanism that grips the recessed hex without slipping on the angled surface. The key is to ensure your wrench doesn't cam out (slip) on the concave face. If you slip, you risk rounding off the bolt head, turning it into a nut driver nightmare where only a large open-end spanner can reach.

Once you have secured the correct socket, apply counter-clockwise torque. Remember, for a reverse thread, "lefty-loosey" still applies to the rotation, but the direction of the wrench handle relative to the bolt axis is inverted compared to a standard bolt. If you are using an impact gun, be extremely cautious. Impact guns rely on rapid hammering blows which can easily strip these softer aluminum or steel plugs if they aren't perfectly seated in the socket. Manual torque with a breaker bar is the preferred approach for this specific hardware.

After removal, inspect the drain plug carefully. Many of these reverse-threaded plugs come with an integrated rubber O-ring seal rather than a flat washer. If you are reusing the old plug, ensure the groove inside the concave head isn't scratched or deformed, as this compromises the seal. When installing the new gasket or O-ring, verify that it sits flush in the recess. A common pitfall is over-tightening these plugs because they feel like they aren't seating properly until the very end of the rotation. Over-torquing a reverse thread plug can crack the aluminum oil pan or strip the threads in the block. Stick to the manufacturer's torque specification, usually around 20â30 lb-ft for Subarus of that era, but never exceed it by guessing.

If you encounter resistance that suggests cross-threading or damage, stop immediately. Forcing it can lead to catastrophic engine oil leaks. In such cases, cleaning the area and potentially replacing the entire drain plug with a new OEM unit is the safest engineering decision. Always verify the thread direction on the replacement part before tightening, as mixing standard and reverse threads is a frequent source of DIY errors that result in stripped bolt heads or gasket failures.
